st.t: Online disputes: Faster processing may not improve justice
st.an: The source establishes that online dispute resolution had become widely available, but it does not assess participation, fairness, representation, accuracy, or substantive outcomes. Its evidence therefore cannot determine whether faster online processing improves justice, though it is consistent with the cluster’s distinction between diffusion and effectiveness.
qs: 96    Online dispute resolution services have become so widely available that an academic journal — The International Journal of Online Dispute Resolution — has been launched to provide practitioners with information about current initiatives and developments.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source provides strong empirical context on modest-value, self-represented state-court litigation and advocates operational case-management reform, which is relevant to selective legal-AI deployment and access-to-justice outcome design. However, it does not evaluate AI capabilities, verification, human–AI collaboration or AI-enabled work redesign, so it cannot establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

kp.k: Historical evidence establishes civil justice conditions before AI
kp.d: This NCSC report examines civil litigation rather than AI. Its empirical foundation is cases disposed between July 1, 2012 and June 30, 2013 across 152 courts in 10 urban counties, comprising over 900,000 cases and approximately five percent of state civil caseloads nationally. The researchers could not generate reliable national estimates because of sample size and weighting complexity; findings describe the participating counties.
qs: The study examined all civil cases disposed in those counties from July 1, 2012 through June 30, 2013.
The resulting dataset included over 900,000 cases
these ﬁndin s report statistics only for the co rts serving these 10 counties.

kp.k: Ordinary civil litigation differs from prominent public debates
kp.d: The authors find that contract and small claims cases dominate the sampled dockets, rather than high-value commercial disputes and tort litigation. Tort cases constitute seven percent of the dataset. They attribute distorted perceptions partly to media attention and the experiences of lawyers and judges concentrated in unusually demanding cases. Medical malpractice and product liability cases together comprise only five percent of tort caseloads.
qs: High-value tort and commercial contract disputes are the predominant focus of contemporary debates
Although tort cases comprise only seven percent of the Landscape dataset
Likewise, judges tend to focus on their experi- ence in cases that demand a great deal of judicial attention

kp.k: Judgments are generally modest, with important measurement limitations
kp.d: For 227,812 judgments exceeding zero, Table 6 reports a mean of $9,267, median of $2,441, and 75th percentile of $5,154. These are recorded judgment amounts, not a complete measure of amounts in controversy. Courts could not identify prevailing parties directly, and equitable relief or counterclaims complicate interpreting positive awards as plaintiff victories. Large awards also skew averages.
qs: The Landscape courts were not able to provide data documenting which party prevailed in cases that resulted in a judgment

kp.k: Litigation economics can undermine access to justice
kp.d: Comparing modest judgments with separate Civil Litigation Cost Model estimates, the authors argue that litigating many ordinary cases through trial costs more than their monetary value. They conclude that representation may be economically unattractive even when claims or defenses have merit. This is an interpretation combining judgment data with other litigation-cost research, not a direct measurement of expenses in every sampled case.
qs: For most represented litigants, the costs of litigating a case through trial would greatly exceed the monetary value of the case.
Indeed, in many cases the cost of litigation likely outstrips the monetary value of the case shortly after initiating the lawsuit.

kp.k: Representation is strongly asymmetric between plaintiffs and defendants
kp.d: Among 649,811 cases in courts reporting both parties' representation status, Table 11 records attorneys representing plaintiffs in 92 percent, defendants in 26 percent, and both sides in 24 percent. The authors argue that this asymmetry challenges assumptions underlying adversarial procedure and raises fairness concerns. They explicitly caution that the data cannot establish firm conclusions about representation's impact in individual cases.
qs: The Landscape data are ins ciently detailed to dra ﬁrm concl sions a o t the impact of attorney repre- sentation in any given case

kp.k: Historical representation comparisons require methodological caution
kp.d: The report contrasts contemporary representation with the 1992 Civil Justice Survey of State Courts, while warning that the definitions differ. The earlier survey counted representation at any point during litigation, whereas the Landscape study followed guidance measuring self-representation at any time, or at disposition when necessary. Consequently, the historical comparison is not a fully equivalent measure of change.
qs: The 1992 Civil Justice Survey of State Courts measured representation status based on whether any party was represented by counsel at any time during the litigation.
The Landscape study employed the State Court Guide methodolo y to meas re representation stat s

kp.k: Small claims procedures may favor represented institutional plaintiffs
kp.d: The authors interpret unexpectedly frequent plaintiff representation in small claims as suggesting that these courts may have become a preferred forum for lower-value debt collection. They express concern that this departs from small claims courts' original purpose as accessible forums for self-represented litigants. This is a qualified inference, not proof that all small claims plaintiffs are debt collectors.
qs: This suggests that small claims courts, which were originally developed as a forum for self-represented litigants to obtain access to co rts thro h simpliﬁed proced res have become the forum of choice for attorney-represented plainti s in lo er val e de t collection cases
Small claims cases are lower-value tort or contract disputes in which litigants may represent themselves without a lawyer.

kp.k: Administrative dispositions dominate, but coding limits precision
kp.d: The report records dismissals for 35 percent of cases, unspecified judgments for 26 percent, default judgments for 20 percent, and settlements for 10 percent. It interprets much of case resolution as administrative rather than formal adjudication. However, dismissals may conceal settlements and unspecified judgments may conceal defaults. Comparisons with 1992 also differ in court coverage and data collection: the earlier study inspected individual files rather than relying on case-management extracts.
qs: Most cases were disposed through an administra- tive process.
a dismissal with prejudice often indicates that the parties have settled the case while a dismissal without prejudice generally indicates either withdrawal or an administrative dismissal.
Consequently, the 1992 data are more accurate and precise than the Landscape data

kp.k: Trial awards reflect selection and extreme outliers
kp.d: The study reports 1,109 jury trials, with bench trials comprising the overwhelming majority of recorded trials. Among trials with positive recorded judgments, Tables 7 and 8 report median awards of $31,097 for 194 jury trials and $1,131 for 11,481 bench trials. The authors interpret the difference as evidence of case selection and caution that large outliers distort means. Missing trial classifications and judgment information restrict these comparisons.
qs: The Miami-Dade Circuit and County Courts and the Marion County Superior and Circuit Courts were not able to identify cases disposed by ench or ry trial

kp.k: Disposition times often exceed national model standards
kp.d: For 820,893 cases with timing data, the mean disposition time was 306 days, the median 113 days, and the 75th percentile 372 days. Overall, 59 percent concluded within 180 days, 75 percent within 365 days, and 82 percent within 540 days. Foreclosures were markedly slower than debt collection cases, and tort cases performed worst among broad categories. The report notes that unusually old cases and administrative closure practices can distort duration statistics.
qs: Some cases in the Landscape dataset had unusually lon disposition times

kp.k: Court data systems constrain measurement and case management
kp.d: The authors identify inconsistent case definitions, organizational structures, counting rules, and operational data priorities as obstacles to comparing courts and understanding outcomes. Systems historically emphasized scheduling and recording events rather than extracting detailed management information. The report argues that inadequate deadline monitoring and limited staff authority leave progress dependent on litigants requesting judicial intervention.
qs: Most case manage- ment systems were initially developed to schedule and record case ﬁlin s and events
they lack the ability to monitor compliance with deadlines or other court orders.

kp.k: Reform requires differentiated procedures and active court oversight
kp.d: The authors argue that uniform procedures can give routine cases more process than they need, while party-controlled pacing and lawyer discretion contribute to delay. They report resistance to mandatory procedural restrictions and underuse of voluntary streamlined programs. Their recommendation is operational reform and stronger court-led case management, rather than procedural rule changes alone.
qs: courts have generally been more attentive to bar demands for control over case management than litigant demands for speedy, just, and inexpen- sive resolution of disputes.
Judges have few incentives to pay attention to those cases that are st ietly pendin on the civil docket.
It is imperative that court leaders move with dispatch to improve civil case management with tools and methods that align with the realities of modern civil dockets

kp.k: Private dispute resolution changes courts' role and professional experience
kp.d: The report describes private ADR competition, contractual arbitration requirements, and online dispute-resolution forums as routes away from public courts. Experienced trial lawyers and retired judges supply private ADR services. The authors warn that declining trials can reduce trial experience within the bar and judiciary, while fewer public adjudications threaten legal precedent and governmental visibility into emerging disputes. These are institutional concerns and proposed mechanisms, not AI predictions.
qs: Ironically, private ADR is often provided by experienced trial lawyers and retired judges.
the growing lack of jury trial experience within the bar and increasingly the state court trial bench.
Fewer common law precedents will leave future litigants without clear standards for negotiating civil transactions or conforming their conduct in a respon- sible manner.
